title: A Late Part Reads Signal Length

scenes.tts: How can one kinase carry two different orders? In a rat cell line called P C twelve, epidermal growth factor, or E G F, says divide. Nerve growth factor, or N G F, says stop dividing and grow nerve-like processes. Both switch on the same kinase, E R K. The molecule is the same, so the difference must lie in something else about the signal.
scenes.visual: A teal kinase chip sits in the middle with two arrows running out to dashed question boxes. EGF arrives and its box becomes 'divide'; NGF arrives and its box becomes 'nerve-like'; both feed the one chip, now named ERK, and question marks mark the unknown difference in each signal.

The molecule is the same, so the difference must lie in something else about the signal.

scenes.tts: E G F switches E R K on briefly, and the cell divides. N G F keeps E R K on much longer, and the cell stops dividing and grows processes. Engineered cells carry extra E G F receptors. Given E G F, they keep E R K active for longer, and they differentiate. So length matters, and the pathway's wiring shapes it.
scenes.visual: The picture opens out into a time plot, one row per signal. ERK activity is drawn as a brief pulse for EGF (outcome: divide), a long plateau for NGF (outcome: nerve-like), and, for EGF in cells with extra receptors, a plateau that is longer than EGF alone but shorter than NGF (outcome: differentiate). Length bars mark each.
scenes.caption: EGF switches ERK on briefly, and the cell divides. NGF keeps ERK on much longer, and the cell stops dividing and grows processes. Engineered cells carry extra EGF receptors. Given EGF, they keep ERK active for longer, and they differentiate. So length matters, and the pathway's wiring shapes it.

scenes.tts: A cell has no stopwatch. What it can do is compare the signal with a delayed product of that same signal. In fibroblasts, E R K switches on a gene called C fos. The C fos protein takes time to make, and once made it is quickly destroyed. So the test is simple: is E R K still on when the new protein appears?
scenes.visual: A stopwatch is crossed out. An ERK signal starts on a time axis; a tag marks that this is in fibroblasts; a long arrow through a c-fos gene chip carries a dot slowly down to a later row, where a c-Fos blob appears after a marked delay and is quickly destroyed. A dashed line drops from the signal at the moment the protein appears, asking whether ERK is still on.
scenes.caption: A cell has no stopwatch. What it can do is compare the signal with a delayed product of that same signal. In fibroblasts, ERK switches on a gene called c-fos. The c-Fos protein takes time to make, and once made it is quickly destroyed. So the test is simple: is ERK still on when the new protein appears?
scenes.narration: A cell has no stopwatch. What it can do is compare the signal with a delayed product of that same signal. In fibroblasts, ERK switches on a gene called c-fos. The c-Fos protein takes time to make, and once made it is quickly destroyed. So the test is simple: is ERK still on when the new protein appears?

scenes.tts: Think of a clinic that calls your name a while after you sign in. Only the people still in the waiting room are seen. If E R K is still active when C fos appears, phosphates are added near one end of the protein. E R K adds them, and so does a kinase that E R K activates. Those phosphates protect C fos.
scenes.visual: The same timeline. The ERK signal turns solid across the moment c-Fos appears; the c-Fos blob appears with a docking tail, two phosphate badges land on the tail, one straight from ERK and one from a second kinase that ERK activates, and a green ring closes round the protected protein.

scenes.tts: After a brief signal, E R K is already off when C fos appears. So C fos is made and lost. After a long signal, E R K is still on, and C fos builds up. As a transcription factor, it can then switch on later genes. So in fibroblasts, C fos lets the cell tell a brief signal from a long one.
scenes.visual: Two panels side by side on the same time axis. Left, a brief ERK pulse ends before c-Fos appears, and the c-Fos blob fades away. Right, a long ERK signal is still on when c-Fos appears, the blobs gain phosphates and pile up, and an arrow leads to a 'later genes' chip. Length bars sit under both signals. The closing line adds a 'in fibroblasts' tag.
scenes.caption: After a brief signal, ERK is already off when c-Fos appears. So c-Fos is made and lost. After a long signal, ERK is still on, and c-Fos builds up. As a transcription factor, it can then switch on later genes. So in fibroblasts, c-Fos lets the cell tell a brief signal from a long one.

scenes.tts: The signal reaches C fos by a fast route and a slow route, and C fos needs both. It needs phosphates from E R K, and it needs the new protein, which takes time to make. This was shown for C fos in fibroblasts, and later for several other early gene products. Do not assume every long signal is read this way. Keep this rule: a part that arrives late can time a signal.
scenes.visual: ERK reaches c-Fos along two unlabelled routes at first, one short and one long through the c-fos gene. The routes are then labelled by what c-Fos needs: phosphates from ERK on the short one, the new protein on the long one. The new protein arrives first and appears as c-Fos; only then do the phosphates travel along their route and dock on it, and a green ring closes. Checks then mark c-Fos in fibroblasts and other early gene products, question boxes follow other long signals, and the late arrival is marked as the part that times the signal.
